findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the ranking rule for a partially-populated index: either cosine ranking requires full current-vector coverage for all live entries (else the query falls back to lexical for the whole corpus with a diagnostic), or define how un-embedded entries are ranked — and add an AC covering a mid-catch-up embedding failure that leaves a mixed index.
evidence: Plan: 'This tier replaces only the scoring function and adds the digest-and-embed build step.'
Plan: 'degrades to lexical whenever one is absent or failing'
ADR 0122 Architecture: catch-up 'processes only tickets whose hash changed or that have no entry' — incremental, so embedding is a per-ticket call that can fail for a subset
src/rebar/similar/catchup via find_similar: catch-up runs in the read path before the query; a mid-build provider failure can leave some entries embedded and some not
Cosine ranking is undefined across entries where only a subset has a vector; the plan's fallback ACs only cover whole-tier absence/failure, not a mixed index
findings.finding: The plan does not specify the ranking behaviour when the index is partially populated — some live tickets carry current vectors and some do not — which is the natural state after a per-ticket embedding call fails or times out mid-catch-up.
findings.location: Approach — 'Ranking swaps behind an interface that already works' and the denial/timeout fallback AC
scenarios: A provider denies or times out after embedding 400 of 630 catch-up tickets; the next query must rank a corpus that is 400-vectored and 230-unvectored
A newly created ticket is indexed lexically but its embedding call fails; a query must decide how to rank it against fully-vectored peers
findings.suggested_fix: State that cosine ranking is used only when every live entry has a current vector for the configured embedding model; if any entry is missing or stale, the query falls back to the lexical tier for the whole corpus (same diagnostic + exit-0 disposition as a provider failure), so results are never ranked across a partially-vectored corpus. Add an AC: a build whose embedding provider fails after N of M tickets leaves the create exit 0 and returns the lexical tier's results.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State (and add an AC asserting) the read-path rule for a partially re-embedded index: only entries whose stored vector matches the current validity key participate in cosine ranking (others fall back to the lexical contribution), so an interrupted re-embed never ranks across two embedding spaces.
evidence: Plan: 'the index's validity key folds the embedding-model identity and the pinned digest-prompt commit in ... Changing either config invalidates and re-embeds the affected entries rather than cosine-ranking across incompatible spaces.'
AC7 acknowledges a provider denial/timeout mid-operation degrades to lexical, so a config-change re-embed can be interrupted with only some affected entries re-embedded.

ABSENCE: no plan sentence or AC states that entries lacking a current-validity-key vector are excluded from cosine ranking (or that the whole tier degrades) while a re-embed is incomplete; the mixed-state read behaviour is unspecified.
findings.finding: After an embedding-model or digest-prompt-commit change invalidates many entries, a re-embed that fails partway (the provider denial/timeout AC7 already acknowledges) leaves the index holding a mix of current-validity-key vectors and invalidated/absent ones; the plan does not state the read rule that prevents the query from cosine-ranking across the resulting old and new embedding spaces, nor an AC asserting it.
findings.location: Approach, "Stored vectors are keyed by what produced them"; AC4 and AC7
scenarios: Operator overrides the embedding model string; catch-up begins re-embedding the now-invalidated entries; the provider times out after re-embedding a subset; the next read queries an index with mixed-space vectors.
A long re-embed is interrupted (process killed) partway, leaving the index persistently mixed until the next successful catch-up.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the 'Stored vectors are keyed by what produced them' section that a query cosine-ranks only over entries whose stored vector carries the current validity key, and add an AC: build an index, change the embedding model, simulate a re-embed that fails after a subset, and assert the query ranks only current-key entries (lexical for the rest) rather than mixing spaces, with the create exiting 0.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile whether the embedding model has an active default (bedrock) or is unset by default, so AC5's 'key unset -> lexical' state is reachable and distinct from AC6's ImportError fallback.
evidence: 'The embedding model defaults to bedrock:amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0'
AC5: 'With no embedding model configured, retrieval returns the lexical tier's results ... when the key is unset'
'This tier is an opt-in ranking upgrade that requires some embedding provider'
findings.finding: The Approach states the embedding model 'defaults to bedrock:amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0' (an active default), but AC5 verifies behavior 'with no embedding model configured' / 'when the key is unset'. If a default model string is always present, the 'unset' state AC5 tests is unreachable in production; conversely if the key is genuinely unset by default, the 'defaults to bedrock' claim is a recommended value, not an active default. The two sections point the implementer in opposite directions on whether the tier is default-on or truly opt-in.
findings.location: Approach ('Both model choices are configuration') vs AC5
scenarios: Fresh install with [bedrock] not installed: does it hit AC5 (unset -> lexical) or AC6 (default bedrock string -> ImportError -> lexical)?
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly: the embedding-model config key is unset by default (tier opt-in); bedrock:amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 is the documented recommended value an operator sets, not a shipped active default.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State, per added fallback arm (missing provider, ImportError, denial/timeout, empty-digest), the disposition it surfaces using an explicit disposition word, and specifically say whether a retryable provider throttle/timeout preserves its retryable disposition (e.g. surfaces WAIT_AND_RETRY/exit-11) or is intentionally masked by the lexical degradation.
evidence: 'This tier is an opt-in ranking upgrade that requires some embedding provider and degrades to lexical whenever one is absent or failing.'
AC: 'When the configured provider raises a denial or times out, retrieval falls back to lexical-only with a diagnostic and the create exits 0.'

The plan distinguishes the digest 'did not answer' state (retried once) from the 'empties' state (falls back, no retry), showing disposition reasoning exists for the digest arm but is not stated with explicit retryable/fatal vocabulary for the provider-failure arm.
ABSENCE: no explicit disposition word (retryable/transient vs fatal/permanent) is attached to the provider denial/timeout arm; rebar's WAIT_AND_RETRY / exit-11 tokens are not referenced.
findings.finding: The plan adds several fallback arms (missing provider, ImportError, provider denial/timeout, empty-digest) that all degrade to lexical-only, but never states each arm's disposition using an explicit disposition word. Most load-bearing: a provider denial-or-timeout is typically a RETRYABLE/transient condition (a throttle/429 that rebar surfaces as exit-11 / WAIT_AND_RETRY), yet the plan silently masks it by degrading to lexical-only. The contract does not say whether that retryable primary disposition is preserved/surfaced or is swallowed by the degradation — the exact 1c0d shape where a retryable primary is masked by a fallback.
findings.location: Approach ('degrades to lexical whenever one is absent or failing') and AC: 'When the configured provider raises a denial or times out, retrieval falls back to lexical-only'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' line: provider denial/timeout is retryable but, because this is an opt-in ranking upgrade, the tier degrades to lexical-only with a diagnostic naming the condition while still letting the create exit 0 — and state explicitly that the retryable disposition is logged (not silently swallowed) so a transient throttle is distinguishable from a permanent absence.
